newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Cadbury may hit acquisition trail.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Cadbury may hit acquisition trail.

text.p: British confectionery and soft drinks group Cadbury Schweppes Plc said on Wednesday it was looking at the possibility of making acquisitions using proceeds from the sale of its stake in Coca-Cola & Schweppes Beverages completed last month.
Chief executive John Sunderland said the 623 million pound proceeds gave Cadbury lots of options to develop its brands organically both in soft drinks and confectionery.
"And of course to acquire any appropriate businesses that we see, be it in beverages or I guess more likely in confectionery," he told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Sunderland said the group would always prefer to pay for any acquisitions from its own resources and said it was unlikely the group would have to tap the market for cash in the near future.
When asked about recent speculation that Anglo-Dutch consumer products group Unilever Plc might make a bid for Cadbury, Sunderland said he shared the market's scepticism about a takeover.

Unilever's decision to sell its speciality chemicals business prompted suggestions that it might bid for Cadbury, but investment analysts have been dismissive about the takeover talk. Sunderland said, "It's not for me to comment, but I'm quite prepared to say that I share the scepticism."

Sunderland said the group's results for 1996 were very strong, and included a good performance from Dr Pepper in the United States, where Cadbury is the third biggest player in soft drinks after Coca Cola and Pepsi.

But Sunderland acknowledged that competition was fierce. He said 7 Up was stabilising after many years of decline. "We've always said that 7 Up is a long term project for us but we regard 1996 as the year in which we stabilised that position."
Cadbury said sales of 7 Up concentrate were ahead so far in 1997 compared to a year ago.
7 Up's market share was slightly down in 1996 by about 0.3 percentage points, but Dr Pepper gained market share and grew faster than the overall soft drinks market in the United States.
European soft drinks were affected by a poor summer in northern Europe, with most markets were flat or down, Sunderland said.
"It wasn't a great year in Europe in the volume sense although...all of our European markets in beverages in profit terms were up with the exception of Portugal," he said.

In Britain, the soft drink market was down slightly against the very hot summer in 1995. But Coca Cola & Scheppes Beverages profits were up three percent, which Cadbury considered very satisfactory give the outstanding summer in 1995.

In confectionery, all Cadbury's core companies had a good year, Sunderland said. In the UK, Cadbury Ltd increased market share for third year in a row, driven by product innovation. Fuse, launched in September, had been in the top three selling countline brands in the UK along with Mars and Kitkat, Sunderland said.
